plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 24: Electric Potential
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a simple three-dimensional drawing of two conducting spheres joined by a wire. A large shaded sphere occupies the upper right of the frame, and a much smaller sphere in the same style sits at the lower left, roughly a third of the diameter of the first. Both are drawn with a soft interior highlight and are ringed by plus signs spaced around their surfaces to indicate positive charge. A thin grey curve sags gently between them, running from the left side of the large sphere down to the right side of the small one and standing for the connecting wire. Each sphere carries a black dot at its center with a short arrow drawn from that dot out to the surface: the arrow in the large sphere is labeled 'R1' and points up and to the right, while the one in the small sphere is labeled 'R2' and points down and to the left. Giving the two spheres markedly different radii while charging both positively is what sets up the comparison. The arrangement, held at a common potential by the wire, is used to relate the surface charge density on each sphere to its radius.

elements: large conducting sphere (soft radial highlight, lavender-grey) in the upper-right of the frame
small conducting sphere (same shading style) in the lower-left, roughly one third the diameter of the large one
black center dot at the center of each sphere
radius arrow from the large sphere's center pointing up-and-right to its surface, labeled R1
radius arrow from the small sphere's center pointing down-and-left to its surface, labeled R2
ring of black plus signs (+) spaced around the visible rim and face of each sphere indicating positive surface charge
thin grey wire drawn as a gently sagging curve from the left side of the large sphere down to the right side of the small sphere
potential label V1 floating near the large sphere
potential label V2 floating near the small sphere
surface charge density readout (sigma value) shown for the currently selected sphere
highlight ring/glow around the selected sphere

interactions.label: R1 / R2
interactions.teaches: At a common potential the surface charge density scales as sigma = eps0*V/R, so shrinking R2 (raising the ratio) visibly crowds the plus signs on the small sphere while the large sphere's signs spread out — charge density is inversely proportional to radius

interactions.label: Wire
interactions.teaches: Connecting the wire forces V1 = V2 and pushes charge onto the larger sphere (denser crowding on the small one); disconnecting it lets the potentials differ, making explicit that the conducting wire is what enforces equal potential
Clicking a sphere highlights its radius arrow and surfaces its local sigma readout, letting the learner directly compare a large R with sparse charge crowding against a small R with dense crowding

demo_steps.title: Connected, ratio 3
demo_steps.narration: Both spheres sit at one potential V1 = V2. The small sphere's plus signs are packed more tightly than the large sphere's, showing sigma proportional to 1/R.

demo_steps.title: Disconnect the wire
demo_steps.narration: With the wire removed the potentials are no longer equal (V1 > V2 for equal surface density) and the charge pattern relaxes toward equal crowding — the wire was what held them at one potential.

demo_steps.title: Increase the ratio
demo_steps.narration: Reconnect and raise R1/R2 to 5: the small sphere shrinks and its plus signs crowd even more densely, dramatizing the inverse sigma-versus-R relationship.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Flat front-on layout (axis_screen_angles null) with 3D-shaded spheres. World span X in [-4,4], Y in [-2,2]. Large sphere center (2.5, 0.7, 0), base radius R1 = 1.2 world units. Small sphere center (-2.7, -0.7, 0), radius R2 = 1.2 / ratio (so ~0.4 at ratio 3). Wire = quadratic/cubic Bezier from large sphere's left rim (~1.3, 0.5, 0) to small sphere's right rim (~-2.3, -0.6, 0) with a control point pulled up-and-mid (~-0.3, 1.1, 0) to give the gentle sag. Plus signs placed on the camera-facing hemisphere: count on each sphere proportional to its charge Q (Q proportional to R when connected), so per-area density proportional to 1/R; when separated use equal density on both. Sphere material: MeshStandardMaterial base #c9c9e2 with a white specular highlight, slight emissive for the soft glow. Plus signs black #111 as small cross sprites/line pairs oriented to face camera. Radius arrows black with arrowhead; R1 arrow direction ~(+0.7,+0.7) in screen plane, R2 arrow ~(-0.6,-0.8). Labels R1, R2, V1, V2 black. Physics: connected -> V1=V2=V0, sigma_i = eps0*V0/R_i; separated (equal sigma0) -> V_i = sigma0*R_i/eps0 so V1/V2 = R1/R2.
interactionPlan.notes: Render spheres as SphereGeometry lit by a key light from upper-left to reproduce the soft interior highlight. Distribute plus signs via a fibonacci-sphere sampling restricted to the front hemisphere (z>0) and project as camera-facing sprites so they read as flat '+' marks like the source. On slider/toggle change, rebuild the plus-sign instanced set and update V1/V2 text and sigma readouts reactively. Keep both spheres' geometry and re-scale via .scale rather than recreating meshes. The selected-sphere highlight is an additive ring sprite plus brightened arrow; clicking empty space deselects. Wire shown only in Connected state (fade out when Separated).

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for radius ratio R1/R2: the learner changes the relative sphere sizes, the plus signs redistribute more densely on the smaller sphere while the wire keeps both at one potential, showing the inverse relationship between radius and surface charge density.

demo_steps.title: Disconnect the wire
demo_steps.narration: With the wire removed the potentials are no longer equal (V1 > V2 for equal surface density) and the charge pattern relaxes toward equal crowding — the wire was what held them at one potential.

demo_steps.title: Increase the ratio
demo_steps.narration: Reconnect and raise R1/R2 to 5: the small sphere shrinks and its plus signs crowd even more densely, dramatizing the inverse sigma-versus-R relationship.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Flat front-on layout (axis_screen_angles null) with 3D-shaded spheres. World span X in [-4,4], Y in [-2,2]. Large sphere center (2.5, 0.7, 0), base radius R1 = 1.2 world units. Small sphere center (-2.7, -0.7, 0), radius R2 = 1.2 / ratio (so ~0.4 at ratio 3). Wire = quadratic/cubic Bezier from large sphere's left rim (~1.3, 0.5, 0) to small sphere's right rim (~-2.3, -0.6, 0) with a control point pulled up-and-mid (~-0.3, 1.1, 0) to give the gentle sag. Plus signs placed on the camera-facing hemisphere: count on each sphere proportional to its charge Q (Q proportional to R when connected), so per-area density proportional to 1/R; when separated use equal density on both. Sphere material: MeshStandardMaterial base #c9c9e2 with a white specular highlight, slight emissive for the soft glow. Plus signs black #111 as small cross sprites/line pairs oriented to face camera. Radius arrows black with arrowhead; R1 arrow direction ~(+0.7,+0.7) in screen plane, R2 arrow ~(-0.6,-0.8). Labels R1, R2, V1, V2 black. Physics: connected -> V1=V2=V0, sigma_i = eps0*V0/R_i; separated (equal sigma0) -> V_i = sigma0*R_i/eps0 so V1/V2 = R1/R2.
interactionPlan.notes: Render spheres as SphereGeometry lit by a key light from upper-left to reproduce the soft interior highlight. Distribute plus signs via a fibonacci-sphere sampling restricted to the front hemisphere (z>0) and project as camera-facing sprites so they read as flat '+' marks like the source. On slider/toggle change, rebuild the plus-sign instanced set and update V1/V2 text and sigma readouts reactively. Keep both spheres' geometry and re-scale via .scale rather than recreating meshes. The selected-sphere highlight is an additive ring sprite plus brightened arrow; clicking empty space deselects. Wire shown only in Connected state (fade out when Separated).

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure is a simple three-dimensional drawing of two conducting spheres joined by a wire. A large shaded sphere occupies the upper right of the frame, and a much smaller sphere in the same style sits at the lower left, roughly a third of the diameter of the first. Both are drawn with a soft interior highlight and are ringed by plus signs spaced around their surfaces to indicate positive charge. A thin grey curve sags gently between them, running from the left side of the large sphere down to the right side of the small one and standing for the connecting wire. Each sphere carries a black dot at its center with a short arrow drawn from that dot out to the surface: the arrow in the large sphere is labeled 'R1' and points up and to the right, while the one in the small sphere is labeled 'R2' and points down and to the left. Giving the two spheres markedly different radii while charging both positively is what sets up the comparison. The arrangement, held at a common potential by the wire, is used to relate the surface charge density on each sphere to its radius.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for radius ratio R1/R2: the learner changes the relative sphere sizes, the plus signs redistribute more densely on the smaller sphere while the wire keeps both at one potential, showing the inverse relationship between radius and surface charge density.
- Toggle between common-potential and separated-spheres views: the learner connects or disconnects the wire, the potential labels equalize only when connected and the charge pattern updates, making clear what the conducting wire enforces.
- Click for selecting either sphere: the learner clicks the large or small sphere, its radius arrow and surface charge density readout highlight, clarifying the comparison between R and local charge crowding.
plan.sourcePath: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 24: Electric Potential

evaluation.notes: The overall composition (two spheres, wire, R₁/R₂ labels) is recognizable, but the critical visual elements — plus signs representing charge, center dots, and radius arrows — are all hidden inside the sphere geometry and invisible in the render, making the figure fail to convey the charge distribution concept visually.
action_items: Move plus signs, center dots, and arrow origins to the sphere surface (z = sqrt(R² - x² - y²) or use a slight outward offset along the sphere normal) so they are visible on top of the sphere mesh
Reduce specular intensity and shininess to match the source's soft, uniform lavender gradient appearance
Ensure the R₁ and R₂ arrows are drawn on top of the sphere surface (e.g., using renderOrder or placing them at the correct z-depth along the sphere surface)
Increase plus sign size slightly and ensure they render in front of the sphere surface
